bracket: [Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2n^2 + 2n + 1\right)\). That is wrong at EVERY \(n\). The correct closed form is \(\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2n^2 + n + 1\right)\). Checked against the series summed term by term: at \(n = 1\) the true sum is \(2\) while the printed form gives \(\dfrac{5}{2}\), which is not even an integer; \(n = 2\) true \(11\) vs \(13\); \(n = 3\) true \(33\) vs \(\dfrac{75}{2}\); \(n = 4\) true \(74\) vs \(82\). The printed form passes 0 of 5 test values; the corrected form passes 5 of 5.]

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key is exactly the closed form of \(\sum r(2r+1)(2r+3)\) — the book used first factor \(r\) where the question prints \(2r - 1\). It AGREES with the true sum at \(n = 1\) (both \(15\)) and diverges from \(n = 2\) onward: true \(120\) vs \(85\), \(n = 3\) true \(435\) vs \(274\), \(n = 4\) true \(1128\) vs \(670\). A spot-check at the first term would certify the wrong answer, which is why several values must be tested. The printed form passes 1 of 5; the corrected form passes 5 of 5.]

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(25\) m. The ball falls \(10\) m and thereafter each rebound height is travelled TWICE — once up and once down — so the total distance is \(10 + 2\left(\dfrac{6}{1 - 0.6}\right) = 10 + 30 = 40\) m, confirmed by direct simulation. The key's \(25 = 10 + \dfrac{6}{1 - 0.6}\) counts each rebound only once, i.e. the ball rises but never comes back down.]

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(800\), which is \(50 \times 2^4\) — the count at the end of the FOURTH hour. Starting from \(50\) and doubling each hour gives \(100, 200, 400, 800, 1600\), so at the end of the fifth hour there are \(1600\) bacteria. What settles it is the book contradicting itself inside this same exercise: Q12 gives the \(n\)th bounce as \(80\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^n\) and Q14 the population after \(n\) years as \(200(1.1)^n\), both putting the exponent equal to the number of periods ELAPSED. Applying that rule here gives \(50 \times 2^5 = 1600\).]

[Textbook misprint: as printed the data are self-contradictory. With \(a = 16\) and sum to infinity \(\dfrac{96}{17}\), we get \(1 - r = \dfrac{16 \times 17}{96} = \dfrac{17}{6}\), so \(r = -\dfrac{11}{6}\) and \(|r| > 1\) — a G.P. whose sum to infinity does not exist, contradicting the question's own premise. With \(\dfrac{96}{7}\) the arithmetic closes cleanly at \(r = -\dfrac{1}{6}\), so the denominator is a misprint. Note the printed key repeats \(-\dfrac{11}{6}\), i.e. it is consistent with the defective stem rather than correct.]

[Textbook misprint: the sequence's fourth term is printed \(\dfrac{-27}{4}\). The book's working only ever uses the first three terms, which is why it never trips over the error.]
